Küche.et: From Middle High German küche, from Old High German chuhhina, from late Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

s: pie; cake; tart (foodstuff made of baked dough, other than bread)
Kuchen.et: From Middle High German kuoche, from Old High German kuohho, from Proto-Germanic *kōkô. Compare Dutch koek. Doublet of Quiche.

Kuckuck.et:
From Middle High German kukkuk, kukuk, gugug; ultimately onomatopoeic.
Compare German Low German Kukuuk, Dutch koekoek, Middle English cukkuk, gokkouȝ (modern English cuckoo).

küchen-.et: At first in Küchenlatein, then generalized. From Küche (“kitchen”), where, in the past, the less educated women and/or house servants would speak among each other.

Küchlein.et: From Middle High German kuchil with the (additional) diminutive suffix -lein. The word was superseded by related Küken, which see for more.

Küchenlatein.et: Compound of Küche (“kitchen”) + -n- + Latein (“Latin”). First attested in Middle Low German köken latyn, Köken latin, thus seemingly a popular word ridiculing the improper use of Latin words by the uneducated (such as women and servants in the kitchen). Later …

Kucera.et: From Czech Kučera, from kučera (“lock of curly hair”).

Kuckuckskind.et: From Kuckuck (“cuckoo”) + -s- + Kind (“child”). After the cuckoo’s habit of leaving its eggs in other birds’ nests.
